lessonRef.title: Concept model B: narrative technique under a formal constraint

studentTask.text: This English 10 lesson develops narrative technique under a formal constraint within the unit “Authorial Structure and Calculated Effect.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's concept model b work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
[1] At the community garden, Owen opened a folder containing a proposal with a margin full of questions. A note on the cover read “Authorial Structure and Calculated Effect,” but the pages inside told one unfinished story. Owen expected the ending to explain everything. Instead, the first scene offered only a quiet choice: return a borrowed object without comment or admit why it had been kept.

[2] The main character rehearsed an apology three times. In the first version, every sentence began with “I.” In the second, the character blamed the confusing rules. In the third, the character named the harm, returned the object, and then stopped talking. The narrator never announced which version was sincere.

[3] Tessa noticed that a repeated image—a door left slightly open—appeared before each rehearsal. At first it seemed like background description. By its third appearance, the image could suggest an invitation, an escape, or an unfinished decision. The story gave enough detail to support more than one interpretation but not enough to make every interpretation equally strong.

[4] The final scene ended before the apology was delivered. Owen argued that the missing speech made the character seem afraid; Tessa thought the pause showed care. To connect the scene to narrative technique under a formal constraint, each reader had to identify exact language, explain an inference, and account for the detail that made the other reading possible.

[5] Before revising, the group tested the source against the workshop goal: narrative technique under a formal constraint. They highlighted language that supported the goal, circled a detail that complicated it, and drew an arrow where the relationship between two ideas needed to be made explicit. The marks produced different possible readings, so the group had to defend priorities rather than copy a single approved answer.

[6] A later reader complicated the discussion by asking about audience and purpose. A concise public notice, a literary interpretation, and a research explanation may use evidence differently even when all three are responsible. The group therefore recorded not only what the source said, but also what situation would make each interpretation effective, insufficient, or misleading.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “Reading Lab 23: narrative technique under a formal constraint”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what narrative technique under a formal constraint asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “Reading Lab 23: narrative technique under a formal constraint,” then answer: Compare the two perspectives or versions in the reading. Which contrast best clarifies narrative technique under a formal constraint, and why?

Deliverable: English 10: a comparison organized around one meaningful contrast; write an analytical response of 300–450 words.

Evidence requirement: Use three precise quotations or paraphrases with paragraph numbers. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If narrative technique under a formal constraint is not yet secure, return to “Reading Lab 23: narrative technique under a formal constraint” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply narrative technique under a formal constraint to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “Reading Lab 23: narrative technique under a formal constraint.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
